entries.title: The ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Filmmakers Terrified Bystanders With Their Monster Sounds
entries.summary: The team behind director Takashi Yamazaki’s new film created their kaiju roars by setting up speakers on top of an outdoor dam. The people walking by weren’t prepared for what they heard.
entries.content:
Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.

While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”

While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.

“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”

Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.

“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”

For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.

Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.

Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.

Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”

During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”

Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.

entries.title: Apple Reboots Its Smart-Home Strategy With New Hardware and a ‘Home Collection’
entries.summary: I got an early glimpse of Apple’s biggest push into the smart home in years.
entries.content:
Apple has lagged in the smart home race, which Amazon and Google have dominated for a decade with Alexa and Google Assistant (now Gemini), respectively.

But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.

That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.

Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras.

Here's everything you need to know.

The Apple HomeView

The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.

It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.)

Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Ask it to open the recipe your friend Alex messaged about, or add a dentist appointment to the family calendar, and it can handle it.

Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. Yes, there’s a camera on the HomeView. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.

We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. It costs $299.

The Apple Home Collection

One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.”

This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).

These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps.

I got a brief look at some of them in action. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. The LG Video Doorbell has two cameras: one to see who is at the door, and one to monitor any packages left at your door.

The LG Outdoor Camera has a floodlight upgrade ($400) that will automatically activate when it detects motion. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off.

The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada.

The HomePod Mini 2

Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. Instead, it has updated the smaller, cheaper sibling: Say hello to the HomePod Mini 2.

The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis.

Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.

One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface.

You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10.

The Apple TV 4K

Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299.

Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Preorders are live now, and it ships November 13.

Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.

If you have ever lost your TV remote, you might be more excited that the new Apple TV 4K remote has built-in Find My support. That means you can ping it in the Find My app or ask Siri for its location, and the familiar AirTag chime will play through the remote's speakers. (It supports ultra-wideband, so you can use Apple's precision-finding mode to locate it between the couch cushions.) The remote is backward compatible, so you don't need the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K if you buy the new remote as a replacement for an older Apple TV.

You can also pair four second-gen HomePod speakers to the new Apple TV 4K, setting two in front of you and two behind you for a surround-sound home theater experience. I heard this in action with two HomePod 2 speakers by the TV and two HomePod Mini 2 models behind the couch—it really does make whatever you’re watching feel more immersive. The speakers calibrate automatically to give you the best sound for your room.

Apple calls this one of the easiest ways to set up a home theater. That four-speaker arrangement would cost you $1,000, but that’s a decent price for a wireless surround-sound system that pairs with all of your Apple products. Just know the surround-sound capability is restricted to specific HomePod models. You're out of luck if you have the original 2017 HomePod or the first-gen HomePod Mini.

The smart-home revamp comes as Amazon and Google both zhuzh their ecosystems by replacing their aging assistants with Alexa+ and Gemini, powered by large language models, which you can think of as a soft reboot. That timing might work in Apple's favor, according to Jitesh Ubrani, director of Consumer Devices Research at IDC.

“Amazon and Google have both reset their platforms with Alexa+ and Gemini, but even their rollouts have been slow,” Ubrani writes in a statement to WIRED. “That means Apple is bringing Siri AI to the home at a point when the competition hasn’t pulled far ahead.”

Apple may finally have the hardware in place, but Siri AI has to prove it belongs in the room.

entries.title: The Apple HomeView Is Like a Giant Apple Watch for the Home
entries.summary: With customizable “faces,” this 7-inch smart display is a unique hybrid between an iPhone and an Apple Watch.
entries.content:
It’s a big year for Apple firsts. The company launched the first MacBook Neo, unveiled its first folding iPhone in September, and installed a new CEO for the first time in 15 years. Now comes the Apple HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.

Rivals like Google and Amazon have made countless screen-enabled smart speakers since voice assistants invaded the home a decade ago. But Apple stuck with a smaller smart home ecosystem centered on its HomePod speakers, even removing the iPad as a hub device a few years ago, which forced users to buy an Apple TV or HomePod to get started. Maybe that’s why it hasn’t found much success in the home.

Announced Tuesday at an event in New York City, the 7-inch smart display arrives alongside several other new smart home devices as part of Apple’s bid to revitalize its lagging ecosystem. The HomeView costs $299 and comes in two versions—a speaker base and a wall-mounted display—both priced the same. Preorders are live, with sales kicking off on November 13.

A Big Apple Watch

The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.

The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.

It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad.

The aluminum hardware, powered by Apple’s A18 chip, comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray (Apple color-matches the woven cable, too). The standard HomeView has a speaker base with a screen that tilts manually up or down for angled viewing, but you can also buy a wall-mountable version. The latter offers three mounts to choose from, one of which is DIY-friendly and has a visible power cord that needs to run to an outlet. The other two are designed for professional installers, either hardwired or connected via Power over Ethernet (PoE).

Technically, the primary speakers—two full-range drivers—are built into the screen. But the standard HomeView has a base that houses a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators for stronger bass. It sounds pretty good based on a very limited listening experience, and can fill a large room quite well. The wall-mounted variant won’t have that extra oomph but Apple claims it tunes the audio for wall placement.

The 7-inch Liquid Retina display has familiar elements, like True Tone, which adjusts the screen’s color temperature to match the room’s lighting. The ambient light sensor can also reduce display brightness from 500 nits to 0.3 nits, which is the lowest brightness Apple has ever engineered on a screen. That’ll be helpful if you place the HomeView on the nightstand.

That is, if you're comfortable placing a camera-equipped display in the bedroom. A 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and four-microphone array sit on the front, but they aren’t just for FaceTime calls. The camera handles facial recognition, allowing the software to adapt to whoever is looking at the screen. Apple says all of this data stays on device.

“Trust is becoming increasingly important with rising consumer expectations around privacy and security,” writes Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint, in an email to WIRED. “In fact, Apple could actually benefit from its privacy-first approach.”

You can add up to six iCloud accounts, and the user interface will adapt to each person, like Google’s Pixel Tablet. That means your wife can tint every app icon green and have no widgets on her home screen, but if you stand in front of the HomeView, it’ll switch to your setup. You won’t be able to view other household members’ sensitive messages and personal information. For this personal content to show up, you don’t just have to stand in front of the HomeView—your iPhone needs to be on the same Wi-Fi network and must have been recently unlocked.

The HomeView can also recognize voices, which helps if Dad asks Siri AI to “Play music.” It will play from Dad’s music library and his preferred music app, rather than another iCloud user’s music. If you have multiple HomePods or HomeViews, you can manage your speaker groups in the HomeView’s interface.

The HomeView also supports Apple’s Handoff tech, so you can bring your iPhone close to send a Safari recipe to the smart display, or have it continue the podcast you were listening to on your commute. In the middle of a FaceTime or phone call? Put your iPhone near the HomeView, and it’ll transfer it over.

Betting on Siri AI

Like any smart display or smart speaker, Siri AI powers the HomeView. It is, after all, the main way to interact with the device (though yes, there’s a keyboard you can pull up to type). Apple spent a great deal of time revamping Siri this year, finally launching a more capable assistant in iOS 27.

Siri AI on the HomeView understands your personal context from your iPhone, so if you ask it to play a song your friend Eric recommended, it’ll know right away what you mean by looking at your Messages history. You can ask when your brother Jeff will likely arrive at your home from the airport on Thursday, then set a schedule for Siri to turn on the coffee maker 15 minutes before his estimated arrival. All of this can be done with natural language, meaning you don’t have to say specific commands for Siri AI to understand you.

One neat trick is the HomeView’s ability to convert recipe pages from Safari into digestible content. Load a recipe, and it will let you view the ingredients or “Start Cooking,” no need to read three paragraphs of the author’s relationship to the stew. It automatically converts the recipe into step-by-step instructions, even auto-populating timers for relevant steps so you can start individual timers as you progress.

Naturally, the HomeView is also designed to control all of your smart home devices, too. You can create a widget for any device you have added in the Home app to quickly control it on the HomeView. And if you swipe to the left from the home screen, you’ll see the “Camera” face, which shows a live stream of connected security cameras (you can view nine feeds at once).

Much like the upcoming iPhone Duo folding phone, Apple is late to market. The company is betting on tight iPhone integration, glanceable Watch-like software, and a more context-aware Siri to make the HomeView feel more like a screen you’ll actually want on your counter. Everything hinges on whether Siri can hold up its end of the bargain—and the voice assistant doesn’t exactly have the best track record.

“The greater challenge is to make AI useful for everyday interactions,” Jain says. “Apple must provide a more capable Siri experience and ensure seamless control across its entire product range in order to stand out from the competition.”

entries.title: 40 Gifts Under $100 That Will Delight Any Tech Enthusiast (2026)
entries.summary: Score a great gift for everyone on your list without breaking the bank. Every one of these gifts comes WIRED-recommended.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Gift shopping on a budget is stressful. Prices can soar around the holidays, making it tough to find genuine bargains. To help, we spent countless hours testing all manner of gizmos and gadgets to bring you expert advice on what is worth buying. These gifts are sure to bring a smile to your loved ones’ faces without breaking the bank too badly, though we know $100 isn't exactly cheap, either.

If you don't mind spending more, check out our Best Tech Gifts guide, and if money is tight, we've also made a list of the Best Gifts Under $25. For giftees with a particular passion, you can find tailored options, like gifts for bird lovers, home chefs, book lovers, and more.

Updated October 2026: I've added 20 new entries and removed several older picks.

  • Portable Sound

    The perfect tiny speaker, the JBL Go 5 fits in the palm of your hand but produces a surprisingly punchy sound with deep bass and clear mids. It's also tough, with an IP68 rating, offers plenty of connectivity options, and boasts battery life of up to 50 hours. It even supports stereo pairing if you have more than one.

    This is the budget pick in our Best Bluetooth Speakers guide.

  • Light It Up

    Govee

    Neon Rope Light Strip 2

    Most light strips are designed to be tucked away in recesses, but this Govee strip has a diffuser, so you can stick it anywhere you want and it still looks great. The adhesive-backed metal brackets make for easy installation. The Govee app allows you to schedule, cycle through colors, play animations, and even create your own scenes. Some transitions are blocky, and the app can be confusing, but this is a great way to introduce your recipient to smart lights.

    This is our favorite diffused light strip from our Best Smart Lighting guide.

  • Power Up

    Nimble

    Champ Portable Charger

    Sling a good portable charger in your bag, and you will never be stranded with a dead phone again. Our favorite is Nimble's Champ, which is compact, light, and packs a 5,000- to 20,000-mAh capacity, capable of recharging most phones and laptops at least once, fully at its smallest size. It comes in snazzy speckled colors with a handy lanyard strap and a small USB-C cable. We are also big fans of Nimble’s environmental efforts (using bioplastics and plastic-free packaging).

    This power bank appears in our Best Portable Chargers guide.

  • A Smart Speaker

    Google

    Home Speaker

    The Google Home Speaker is our favorite smart speaker right now. It boasts impressive sound for its small form, the AI is a little more human than competitors, and it comes in a range of fun colors. Gemini is also helpful and smart, though some of the best features require a subscription.

    This speaker is the top pick in our Best Smart Speakers guide.

  • Desk Tidy

    Oakywood

    Headphone Stand with Wireless Charger

    We love multifunctional gadgets like this headphone stand from Oakywood, which offers a place to hang your cans and a spot to wirelessly charge your phone. The angular base in solid walnut or oak is super stylish, and the steel stand keeps your headphones neatly out of the way.

    This headphone stand appears in our Best Wireless Chargers guide.

  • Game On

    Backbone

    One

    Comfy to hold for long gaming sessions, with a subtle texture that adds grip, this mobile controller combines responsive analog sticks with clicky buttons and an excellent D-pad. It cradles your phone with a built-in USB-C connector for a speedy connection and includes pass-through charging, a screenshot or screen-recording button, a mute button, and a headphone jack. There's also a handy companion app with an optional subscription.

    This is a top pick in our Best Mobile Controllers guide.

  • Motion Sensor

    Kinisium

    Kini SafeAlert Wi-Fi Motion Sensor

    This versatile motion sensor can flag access to a cabinet, drawer, or safe. You can easily configure it in the app to set exactly what triggers an alert, set the cooldown period, and choose how you want to receive alerts. Unlike many other smart home devices, it keeps everything private.

    This gadget appears in our Best Motion Sensors guide.

  • Forty Winks

    LectroFan

    Evo Sound Machine

    I have a constant whining tinnitus sound in my ears after a misspent youth of loud gigs and clubs. A white-noise machine helps me tune it out at night so I can drop off to sleep. This is what I have on my nightstand right now, and it works great. Compact, easy to use, and with 22 non-repeating sounds (I like the ocean surf) and a timer function, it's all you need.

    This gadget appears in our Best Sound Machines guide.

  • Wireless Keyboard

    Keychron

    B2 Pro

    One of the best scissor-switch keyboards available, the Keychron B2 Pro offers a comfortable, quiet typing experience, is fully customizable (you can use Keychron’s Launcher software to remap keys and set up macros), and looks pretty stylish.

    You’ll also find this deck in our Best Keyboards guide.

  • Gaming Mouse

    SteelSeries

    Rival 3 Gen 2

    You don’t have to spend big to snag a great gaming mouse, and the SteelSeries Rival 3 proves it. This mouse is lightweight and responsive, with a lovely rubbery scroll wheel and a couple of handy side buttons. It’s everything most people need without the unnecessary frills.

    This is the budget pick in our Best Gaming Mice guide.

  • Excellent Earbuds

    JLab Audio

    Go Pop ANC

    Solid sound, active noise cancellation that works well, stable Bluetooth connectivity, a robust app with adjustable EQ and programmable controls, and a respectable IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating—these full-featured earbuds have it all.

    These are the cheapest option in our Best Wireless Earbuds guide.

  • Charging Station

    Tessan

    Cat Charger

    This feline charging block is so cute. The cat's face changes when it's on standby and charging, and the screen can show the total outgoing wattage and break it down by port (it maxes out at 65 watts). There are two USB-C and two USB-A ports to plug in all your small gadgets.

  • Coffee to Go

    Hydro Flask

    Coffee with Flex Sip Lid

    With a practically indestructible powder coating, this travel mug is ideal for folks seeking a low-maintenance mug that doesn't need careful handling. It also has a pebbled texture that adds grip, and it holds plenty of coffee.

    This is the top pick in our Best Travel Mugs guide.

  • Head Light

    Ledlenser

    MH10 LED Headlamp

    Whether you're walking the dog at night, working on a PC or a car engine, or looking for something in the basement, a headlamp like this keeps your hands free and provides plenty of light (600 lumens) where you need it. The battery lasts at least 10 hours on a full charge.

entries.title: 30 Best Tech Books to Gift in 2026: Biographies, Startup Histories, Exposés
entries.summary: Give the techie in your life access to the inner workings of the companies and characters shaping Big Tech.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

It is tough to overestimate Big Tech’s influence on the modern world. But how did we get here? The best tech books unravel the rise and, occasionally, fall of some of the dominant companies and characters that created the gadgets and software we spend so much of our lives using.

You’ll find intensely detailed biographies, in-depth company histories, and plenty of drama and enlightenment in these tech tomes, and they also make great gifts for the techy folks in your life. You may also be interested in our Gifts for Book Lovers, Best Cookbooks, and Best Kindles guides.

Updated October 2026: I added five books, including Apple in China, More Everything Forever, Gouged, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and The Nerd Reich.

  • Chip Chase

    The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip

    by Stephen Witt

    Charting Nvidia’s rise to become one of the most valuable companies on earth, this biography of cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang is educational and entertaining. Witt explains how the company spun GPU (graphics processing unit) manufacturing for gaming into parallel processing and a marriage of hardware and software that has powered the rise of AI. It has also made Huang very rich, but he isn’t always painted in a flattering light, which helps to counterbalance the founder worship vibe.

    For a slightly different view on Nvidia's history, try The Nvidia Way: Jensen Huang and the Making of a Tech Giant, by Tae Kim.

  • The Early Days of the Computer

    The Soul of a New Machine

    by Tracy Kidder

    A well-deserved winner of the Pulitzer Prize, this book should be required reading for anyone who works in technology or harbors a curiosity about how it came to dominate our lives. First published in 1981, the book reveals the inner workings of Data General in the 1970s as the company strives to design and release a successful next-generation minicomputer. Kidder captures the struggle between management and creatives and weaves a fascinating tale from an ostensibly dry subject. He explains the intense time pressure on engineers that led to a constant state of crunch, the need for recruits to feel like they are working on something important they have some stake in, and the psychology of leadership intent on realizing ambitious projects. It is positively prescient about the dangers of burnout for the unsung heroes who sacrifice so much to build new machines.

    Follow this up with WIRED’s article chatting with some of the subjects in the book 20 years after it was published (this article itself is now more than 20 years old).

  • Evil Twin

    Doppelganger: A Trip Into the Mirror World

    by Naomi Klein

    This fascinating dive down the rabbit hole of Covid conspiracy is ostensibly about how people confuse Naomi Klein with Naomi Wolf. Klein is a leftist journalist and climate activist; Wolf was a third-wave feminist but is now a rabid anti-vaxxer.

    If you’re still puzzled over the convergence of wellness and the far-right or wondering why so many ordinary folks are swallowing the kind of misinformation that breeds racism and climate denialism, Klein has some convincing answers. This is challenging and sometimes bleak reading, but it was also the most important book of 2023. It's brutally honest, calling out the absurdities of capitalism and the role social media has played in the rise of narcissism.

  • An Icon

    by Walter Isaacson

    Released just 19 days after the death of Apple cofounder Steve Jobs, this astonishing biography takes a deep dive into his life and goes some way toward explaining his enduring legacy. Isaacson was picked by Jobs himself, who granted more than 40 interviews to his biographer and reportedly exerted no control over the final edit. Jobs’ intense passion and ambition saw him successfully marry creative ideas with technological innovations and sell them to the general public. This is an accessible book that never gets too technical. It insightfully charts the rise of Apple and Pixar and the development of the Mac, iTunes, the iPhone, and the iPad. While it is flattering at times, Jobs’ ruthlessness is not sugar-coated, and anyone with more than a passing interest in the man must read this book.

    For a less Jobs-centric exploration of the Mac’s development, read Revolution in The Valley: The Insanely Great Story of How the Mac Was Made, by Andy Hertzfeld.

  • Cancel Culture

    So You've Been Publicly Shamed

    by Jon Ronson

    The dark side of the internet’s hive mind is brought into sharp relief by Ronson’s cast of characters—all have been publicly shamed via the internet. From the fascinating tale of Jonah Lehrer’s plagiarism to the vilification of Justine Sacco after an ill-advised joke tweet decried as racist, Ronson digs into the stories behind the scandals and looks at the havoc relentless online shaming can wreak. The book is a fun and fascinating look at how shame, empowered by social media, is a forceful form of social control with real-life consequences.

    Jon Ronson is my favorite non-fiction writer, and I also highly recommend The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men and The Psychopath Test: A Journey Through the Madness Industry.

  • Made in China

    Apple in China: The Capture of the World's Greatest Company

    by Patrick McGee

    Who would have thought that maximizing profit at any cost might lead to problems? Apple’s pursuit of every cent led it to outsource virtually all of its gadget production to China, and now it’s grappling with the economic, political, and cultural fallout. McGee has spoken with many former Apple executives and engineers to uncover what happened, why, and what it means for Apple and the US.

  • Google’s Machinings

    In the Plex: How Google Thinks, Works, and Shapes Our Lives

    by Steven Levy

    I could have easily included a few entries from WIRED's own Steven Levy on this list, from his hugely influential 1984 debut, Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution, to his most recent release, Facebook: The Inside Story, but I’ve chosen In the Plex. Despite the impact of Google, a company whose name has become a verb, most of us know little about its internal workings. This is the best book to read if you want to change that. Levy secured unprecedented access to serve up a fascinating dive into what makes Google tick, what drove successful expansion into new areas, and how the company and its products have changed the world.

    If you want more, How Google Works, by Eric Schmidt and Jonathan Rosenberg, offers some insight into management at the company.

  • Resisting Big Tech

    The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation

    by Cory Doctorow

    I remember when the internet was good, before we got trapped in walled gardens and Big Tech put the thumbscrews on us to extract every last cent. Cory Doctorow’s wonderfully evocative “theory of enshittification” is widely accepted now and increasingly common everywhere you look. He reckons that interoperability might just be the antidote, and while his sharp critiques are more fully formed than his suggested solutions, at least he’s trying to offer some hope.

  • The Rise and Fall of Theranos

    Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup

    by John Carreyrou

    Noble aims and raw ambition are lauded in the tech world, often attracting praise and investment, but what happens when a project goes wrong?

    Building on Wall Street Journal reporter Carreyrou’s shocking exposé of Theranos, this book follows charismatic founder Elizabeth Holmes as she tries and fails to build a blood testing machine to sweep away the need for hypodermic needles, with the promise of accurate tests done from a drop or two of blood via a pinprick on the finger. Although the company raised hundreds of millions of dollars, its technology was horribly inaccurate. Rather than admit defeat, it pressed on, which is why Holmes was put on trial for fraud and sentenced to 11 years in prison. The book highlights the dangers of the popular “fake it till you make it” approach. Theranos reached a paper valuation of $9 billion and employed more than 800 people before its spectacular fall.

  • Broligarch Bashing

    More Everything Forever: AI Overlords, Space Empires, and Silicon Valley's Crusade to Control the Fate of Humanity

    by Adam Becker

    Silicon Valley ideology and the self-serving narratives of tech billionaires are exposed as delusional rationalizations for the crazed accumulation of wealth and power in this fascinating, reasoned, sometimes depressing, but always well-argued book. Becker does his homework thoroughly to debunk our immoral CEO overlords and the philosophies and movements they espouse.

  • Generative AI

    You Look Like a Thing and I Love You: How Artificial Intelligence Works and Why It's Making the World a Weirder Place

    by Janelle Shane

    If you can't help but ponder about artificial intelligence these days, you'll get a kick out of this book. It delves into machine-learning algorithms and their limitations in an accessible, engaging, and often hilarious way.

    Shane is the research scientist behind the comical AI Weirdness blog, and she does a solid job of demystifying AI, explaining how machine learning really works, and highlighting its strengths and weaknesses. Although you’ll learn about things like generative adversarial networks, the book never gets dull, thanks to witty and moreish writing peppered with practical examples of AI attempts at creativity that are frequently laugh-out-loud funny.

  • Power Shifts

    The New New Thing: A Silicon Valley Story

    by Michael Lewis

    Opening on a computerized superyacht, the talented Michael Lewis takes us on an adventure into the mind of billionaire Jim Clark, cofounder of Netscape and Silicon Graphics. The book charts the power shift in Silicon Valley startups from “money men” to “idea men” and engineers.

    Lewis also attempts to uncover what drives Clark’s endless pursuit of the next thing and his seemingly unquenchable desire for more. This modern captain of industry is restless, constantly dissatisfied, and not very likable. The voyage is an interesting frame, and there are echoes of Kidder’s book in its subject’s idiosyncrasies and the author’s earnest attempt to explore what truly motivates him.

  • AI Race

    Supremacy: AI, ChatGPT, and the Race That Will Change the World

    by Parmy Olson

    The race to make AI mainstream is framed as a battle between CEOs, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Demis Hassabis of DeepMind, but Olson does a good job of showing how seeming idealists with good intentions can be swayed by billionaires and end up selling out. If you wonder about the forces fueling the AI arms race, how bloated valuations have led to political power, or the laundry list of ethical and legal concerns AI raises, you’ll find this book enlightening.

  • Silicon Valley

    The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America

    by Margaret O'Mara

    If you have ever wondered how such a small suburban area came to dominate the tech world, Margaret O’Mara, a history professor at the University of Washington, has some answers. This concise and comprehensive book weaves together interviews, biographies, and countless other sources to explain how Silicon Valley has driven and dominated technological innovation. O’Mara exposes the foundations that self-mythologizing founders and businesses are built on, and the vital role the government played in their rise.

    Folks seeking an insider’s view might like Uncanny Valley: A Memoir, by Anna Wiener.

entries.title: Wikipedians Believed AI Would Come and Go. They Were Wrong
entries.summary: In a world of AI Overviews, Wikipedia usage declines. But the real loss may be far more existential than website traffic.
entries.content:
Long before the storm of AI struck Wikipedia, the Wikimedia Foundation was making preparations. Wikipedians battened down the hatches and made confident-sounding predictions that it would break and wash over them. Large language models might even improve Wikipedia, it was said, automating more of the housekeeping—formatting, sources, citations, missing links—and so freeing up humans to do creative work. It was not so simple. In 2019, then-Wikimedia Foundation head Katherine Maher wrote an op-ed in The New York Times under the headline “Without Humans, A.I. Can Wreak Havoc.” “Too often,” she wrote, “artificial intelligence is presented as an all-powerful solution to our problems, a scalable replacement for people.” The issue confronting Wikipedia, retaining human control over machines, was the same one soon being faced everywhere.

Already in 2018 Google was training AI to write “Wikipedia-like articles,” and by October 2024, a Princeton University study found that about 5 percent of nearly 3,000 newly created articles on English Wikipedia in a single month (August 2024) contained a substantial amount of AI-generated content. There were signs. ChatGPT was fond of em dashes—parenthetical statements that look like this one—and curly quotation marks. Sometimes, residues from the prompts used to compose articles were left behind (“Here is your Wikipedia article,” they might say.)

At first, Wikipedians tried to shape and control AI, to make its output “acceptable and constructive,” or to fix or remove if it proved otherwise. Generic fluff like “praising a village for its fertile farmlands, livestock, and scenic countryside” and fake sources were weeded out. By March 2026, AI content was found to violate its core principles so often that writing with large language models was banned outright, and their role restricted to translation and minor proofreading.

A much-read essay titled “Death of Wikipedia” explained this defensive posture. It predicted a ripple effect: As contributors reduced their contributions in response to AI pervading the platform, there might be a temptation to replace their work with still more AI, creating a downward spiral. One viral X post lamented that artificial intelligence seemed to be changing things in the wrong direction: “I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do art and writing, not for AI to do my art and writing so that I can do my laundry and dishes.” The “Death of Wikipedia” warned against something similar: Rather than AI performing Wikipedia’s “housekeeping” roles, it might compose its articles instead, leaving humans relegated to formatting and cleanup. The result would trap editors in an endless curatorial project derived not from human priorities but from the frostbitten harvests of machines.

“The potential ‘whittling down’ each year of our pool of talented writers is the greatest threat to Wikipedia,” another Wikipedian wrote, “as we must increase the number of editors, especially expert editors, to be able to fix the sprawling hellscape of weak, inaccurate and incomplete articles that drag down the project.” A Wikipedia written and read by machines threatened to create a new, deracinated Wikipedia, stripped not only of its context, but of its animating passion. It would be artless, and soulless. When the Wikimedia Foundation says that the care and commitment of Wikipedians to “reliable encyclopedic knowledge is something AI cannot replace,” that is not the same as saying that it will not be replaced.

Once Google introduced AI Overviews in search, they quickly became as central to the experience as Wikipedia was until recently. (This also means Wikipedia still does play a crucial role as a source, only at one step removed.) Anyone who uses AI agents knows that they give plausible, almost intuitive answers, which can pass a superficial review of their sourcing. They are also often wrong. If Wikipedia itself becomes corrupted by artificial intelligence, by what means will we prove when they are wrong?

Implicit in the idea of a single, machine-edited encyclopedia to rule them all is that such a phenomenon should act as a final authority. Its appeal, to the kind of people who find it appealing, is that it will be coolly rational, a kind of digital King Solomon that can act as a disinterested arbiter. There is no reason to think such cold logic would not be cruel instead. Its aesthetic failings are a clue: “Slop” is a useful word for the product of artificial intelligence, which implies something unvariegated and monotonous, absent not only of nutritional value but also of the flavor that makes nutrition a pleasure.

There is also no reason to believe an AI encyclopedia, or any other encyclopedia, should be unifying. Whatever its shortcomings and eccentricities, Wikipedia is the closest thing to an “encyclopedia of everything” we have ever had. Once smartphones became widespread after the iPhone’s launch in 2007, the old speculations, however far-reaching, were realized: Wikipedia was costless, portable, immediate, and electric. Enormous and omnipresent, it really became an approximation of the “sum of all human knowledge.” But so what? What did access to this oracle mean for human flourishing? What good has Wikipedia done?

A documentary maker, wanting to bring Wikipedia’s story to the screen, asked me a sharpened version of this question. Yes, Wikipedia was the little encyclopedia that could. It had overcome humble origins to become massive. But the dictates of streaming television needed something more. Were there, she asked, any real-life episodes where Wikipedia had “saved the village”? Has Wikipedia saved lives? The answer is “probably,” though not in dramatic or famous ways. Quick-fire encyclopedic knowledge has helped with accidental poisoning, and there are signs that Wikipedia is accessed with special frequency during natural disasters. But these anecdotes are difficult to corroborate, and often, when Wikipedia’s role is scrutinized, it turns out to be incidental. If someone calls for help in an emergency, it is not the phone which is the hero.

Does Wikipedia perform a public good? This seems self-evident but is much harder to measure and, in a way, is out of the project’s hands. In 2013, when an online poster posed the question “If someone from the 1950s suddenly appeared today, what would be the most difficult thing to explain to them about life today?” the top answer went viral as a mordant sign of the times: “I possess a device, in my pocket, that is capable of accessing the entirety of information known to man. I use it to look at pictures of cats and get in arguments with strangers.” Elsewhere, the “arguments with strangers” line was expressed in less lighthearted ways. “The greatest threat to democracy may no longer derive from human agency but from new forms of technology, which have the capacity to undermine democracy without anyone having intended it,” the academic David Runciman wrote two years later. “The forces from which democracy needs rescuing are no longer pressing on it from the outside. They come from within.”

No one is credited with foreseeing Wikipedia more clearly than H. G. Wells, a reputation built on a series of essays collected in his book World Brain, and its advocacy for a “Permanent World Encyclopaedia.” But Wells expounded on this idea many times, and his other writings were much more equivocal, and he even satirized his own obsessions in The Camford Visitation: “He wants a universally educated world, educated on the same lines, with every artificial difference eliminated. He is a cantankerous, disagreeable little nobody and yet at times one feels he has got hold of something most exasperatingly vast and right.” Soon after World Brain was published, Wells had lost faith in his encyclopedic vision altogether and succumbed to late-life pessimism. Humanity had orchestrated to create a world war, not a world brain, and in the civilizational race between “education and catastrophe,” as he put it, catastrophe looked to have a winning lead.

Less obvious to us now is that World Brain was also an antidote. The most significant new European encyclopedias that preceded it, the Great Soviet Encyclopedia and the Enciclopedia Italiana, were direct expressions of nationalist and totalitarian intent, so much so that the entry on “Fascism” in the Enciclopedia Italiana was credited to Benito Mussolini himself. Wells understood that “internationalism” needed its own encyclopedia as a counterweight, but that did not make it a simple force for freedom. He assumed that the World Brain would assist a world government in projecting its power, and though democratically available, his Permanent World Encyclopaedia would make such a world government omnipotent. A world government that was all-seeing as well as all-knowing would inevitably be repressive; a sinister side to Wells’ ideas seemed to have partly inspired George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four.

Orwell also critiqued Wells more explicitly in his 1941 essay “Wells, Hitler, and the World State.” One of its more perceptive observations is that Wells was not, in fact, a futurist. He was a nostalgic, Orwell thought, a “nineteenth-century liberal” who had spent 40 years repeating the same idea: that history was a battle between “the man of science who is working towards a planned World State” and “the reactionary who is trying to restore a disorderly past.” With Orwell’s help, we can see that Wells’ World Brain was an old idea, not a new one. Versions of it had preexisted Wells by centuries, and this particular encyclopedic worldview sprang from his Edwardian conception of Progress with a capital P.

The encyclopedia handed down to us from the Enlightenment is much more than a collation of facts in a book or on a website. It is a whole mode of seeing and doing, a lens through which a clear, scientific vision of all things can come into view, unobstructed by superstition. Witness the world in this way, and the world changes. So far-reaching is this idea that the philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre classed “encyclopaedia” as one of the three major approaches of Western ethics, what he called “rival versions of moral enquiry.” The others were “tradition,” starting with Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle, and “genealogy,” which began with Nietzsche. Tradition was a marriage of faith and reason. Genealogy emphasized hidden power relations. Encyclopaedia relied on reason alone, trying to build an objective picture of the world that could determine how to act, thanks to a consensus version of the truth. The purest expression of this was to be found in the 19th century, in the ninth edition of Encyclopaedia Britannica, which promised “the available facts of human history, collected over the widest areas … carefully coordinated and grouped together, in the hope of ultimately evolving the laws of progress, moral and material, which underlie them.”

When Three Rival Versions of Moral Enquiry was published in 1990, MacIntyre’s notion was already criticized for being out of date. One reviewer complained that it saddled “the encyclopaedists with their 19th-century dogmatic statements in Britannica and plays down the fact that few if any of their heirs hold such views today.” Yet there were some places that rational-liberal outlook did survive in an unapologetic form. It remained at the very forefront of Encyclopaedia Britannica—the 1987 edition opened with the motto of its associate, the University of Chicago: “Let knowledge grow from more to more and thus be human life enriched.” Most pertinently, it undergirded the beliefs of Wikipedia’s cofounders. Not only did Wikipedia’s text-heavy format reflect a centuries-old Enlightenment tradition, it was also created by two men who still believed, earnestly, that discovering the facts and learning lessons from them was not only the purpose of an encyclopedia, but the central task of a life well lived.

The divergent paths of Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger offer a kind of parable for the fate of this worldview and the cultural crosscurrents that swamped it. Twenty-five years after Wikipedia’s founding, Wales is still a Davos Man, an international person for an international project, who lives in the capital of the United Kingdom and makes frequent criticism of the MAGA movement. Sanger never left Ohio, where he homeschooled his children, became a vocal vaccine skeptic during the Covid-19 pandemic, and voted for Donald Trump. In 2025, he announced that he had given up his long-standing agnosticism to become a professing Christian, and wrote a book-length philosophical proof for the existence of God. If Wales remained wedded to the MacIntyre-style notion of “encyclopedia”—Enlightenment rationalism, with an added Objectivist trim—Sanger had returned to “tradition.”

As Wikipedia affirmed its status as a knowledge institution, it also lost its immunity from the crises afflicting knowledge institutions everywhere. The only surprise was that it had been exempt for so long. At the end of her tenure as head of the Wikimedia Foundation, Sue Gardner had likened the experience to living on a peaceful tropical island as “cruise missiles flew overhead.” Culture war had broken out all around, and now Wikipedia was an island no more. In the 2010s, “disinformation,” “misinformation,” and “fake news” were all selected as words of the year in short order, and the saturation of information was just as blameworthy as its corruption. Instead of adjudicating between facts like judges, audiences acted like lawyers assembling a brief and took only what they wanted. The results of “doing your own research,” an off-kilter version of the Enlightenment demand “dare to know,” were algorithmically personalized pseudo-informational systems. Mired in this uncertain environment, Wikipedia approached its 25th anniversary facing unprecedented political, cultural, and technological threats.

All of this added an elegiac note to its birthday celebrations in January 2026. The Pew Research company marked the occasion by quantifying the encyclopedia’s staggering reach—in the decade between 2015 and 2025, Wikipedia had been viewed 1.9 trillion times, an average of 508 million views per day. These immense numbers nevertheless contained an unmistakable arc of decline. In the days prior to the anniversary, a long-time Wikipedian, Christophe Henner, published a long and detailed “wake-up call” for the Wikipedia movement. Since 2022, the encyclopedia had lost almost a quarter of its readership, more than 1.1 billion visits per month, a missing audience who, presumably, were seeking out AI summaries instead. Even when answers offered by AI agents contain links, readers tend not to follow them: One figure showed that the click-through rate from AI chatbots was only 0.33 percent; for the Google search engine, it had been closer to 9 percent. For a model whose lifeblood was readers becoming editors, it was a disaster.

Artificial intelligence was an existential risk to Wikipedia, Henner warned, and the encyclopedia risked being remembered as a “historical artifact that AI once trained on … a footnote in the training data of models that have moved on without us.” An editing crisis meant that fewer and fewer editors were performing more and more labor, “a smaller club working harder to maintain something fewer people see,” as he put it. Past moments of opportunity—for example, when Wikipedia might have harnessed the growth of the internet outside Western countries—had mostly been squandered. The energy generated by places like India and Nigeria going digital had passed Wikipedia by, and in the wake of all this, the encyclopedia risked becoming a “temple,” maintained by the last in a priest class of superannuated Wikipedians. Once sacrilegious ideas, like paying editors for their work, had to be considered anew. Otherwise, the whole of Wikipedia might be reduced to an abandoned cathedral.

Media coverage marking the occasion was just as bittersweet. In Nature, Dariusz Jemielniak wrote that “academic indifference” and artificial intelligence threatened Wikipedia’s survival, accusing agentic AI of exploiting a “parasitic relationship” that “endangers the last bastion of freely accessible, human-curated knowledge and undermines the premise of collaboration on which many of Wikipedia’s knowledge-sharing practices rely.” “Wikipedia’s Existential Threats Feel Greater Than Ever” was the headline for a Stephen Harrison piece in WIRED, a catalog of threats beleaguering the project. More dangerous than hostile think tanks and lawmakers was an increasingly indifferent public, slowly drifting away from its founding ideals. “Economic precarity [has] trained many Gen Zers to see any unpaid labor as a scam,” Harrison wrote. In the cold light of the dawning era, becoming a Wikipedia super editor during a period of unemployment seemed a distant luxury, or outright perplexing, “thankless work that AI companies strip-mine for a profit.”

The tide turning on Wikipedia was more than the advent of artificial intelligence or a fragmentation of reading habits. Christophe Henner thought the “AI summaries” were only a “convenient explanation.” “I’m skeptical,” he wrote:

Even this undersold the quantum of change. Something far older was fast losing relevance as well: It was the beginning of the end of the encyclopedic age. Near the front of the French Encyclopédie there is a diagram called the “figurative system of human knowledge,” which is now sometimes called “The Tree of Diderot and d’Alembert.” The Tree is a system for not only ordering “the parts of knowledge,” but connecting them in a logical chain so long it can wreath the universe. It represents a bold idea: that an encyclopedia’s unifying force will show how everything in existence is linked. It suggests that knowing everything will lead to knowing One Big Thing about everything. This old-fashioned idea was resuscitated in the computer age, and gathered momentum with the concept of AGI, artificial general intelligence, the moment machines surpass every form of human understanding. If realized, it will represent not only the end of encyclopedias, but their culmination. Human-written encyclopedias will still exist after AGI, but only as secular scriptures in the mind of a digital god.

The longest-standing critique of “encyclopaedia” is religious: It is the belief that human activity on a godlike scale is a doomed act of conceit. It was only during the Enlightenment that absolute knowledge came to be considered beneficial (and today, “know-it-all” is still an insult, not a compliment). Beforehand, desire for absolute knowledge was viewed as a sin or a crime, a proscription that continues in many cultures. Greek mythology is full of cautionary figures like Pandora and Prometheus, who knew too much and suffered for it; when the Norse god Odin seeks the sacred well waters granting wit and wisdom, a single drink costs him one of his eyes. In the very first book of the Bible, two different stories, the Tower of Babel and the Garden of Eden, carry variations on the same moral: Total understanding must be God’s alone. Curiosity is not only a sin, but the first sin.

One of the many artworks inspired by Wikipedia speaks to this phenomenon. In the 2010s, the bio-artist Joe Davis declared that he would engineer a real, living Tree of Knowledge, the tree described in the Bible that holds forbidden fruit and results in the fall of humankind. To do so, Davis planned to take a 4,000-year-old strain of apple trees and copy the English-language edition of Wikipedia into the letters of its DNA. He called the project Malus ecclesia, which in Latin is a pun that means both “evil church” and “apple tree church.” In interviews, Davis refused to say whether he would eat the Tree’s fruit; because of laws around genetic modification, ingesting an apple or even planning to may have been a criminal act. Mired in red tape, this tantalizing idea never came to fruition, but its forbidding message remains: The sum of all knowledge is cursed.

The real existing Wikipedia feels less melodramatic than that, and the most lasting dividend of Wikipedia may not be its contents but its process, which holds a promise quite unlike the Tree of Knowledge or even the Tree of Diderot. For years, the annual Wikimania conference has sustained a fledgling tradition: At the opening ceremony, Wikipedians wear their national dress. When almost three-quarters of the nations on earth are in attendance, this produces a real spectacle, even against a backdrop of convention center carpet. All around the room are people wearing hanboks and kaftans and kimonos (the practice was initiated by a Japanese Wikipedian), and when they intermingle, the effect is like those old, quaintly hopeful pictures canvassing the “Peoples of the World.” Appreciating the depth and variety on display takes longer. Those golden headdresses, called serimpak, are worn by the seafaring tribes of Borneo, and that is why they are shaped like ships. The chapan robes that seem to swirl under their resplendent colors are from central Asia; those heavy ponchos, overkill against the air-conditioning, have come all the way from the Andes. Someone offers Jimmy Wales a conical nomad’s hat from Burkina Faso, but he cannot accept all the paraphernalia presented to him. There is too much.

Those might be lederhosen in the distance, although someone jokes that the real German national dress is sandals with socks. At least one tech type seems to be wearing Hawaiian shorts for a similar reason, as the official livery of Silicon Valley. Everywhere there is embroidery, silk and brocaded colors, headscarves and skullcaps, a pageant of signs and patterns from parts unknown. Once congregated, the people wearing this garb do not generate an atmosphere of hubris. In this room their shared mission seems humble. Their talk is the slow, uncertain work of mutual understanding, graced with the tentative socializing of the shy. They are bounded by human fallibility, the same thing that ennobles them. Together, they call to mind a Latin phrase very different from Malus ecclesia. E Pluribus Unum—out of many, one.
